# Public transport routing with `r5r` {#sec-m4-gtfs}

For cars (@sec-m4-roteamento), the cost of an edge is fixed: length divided by
speed. For public transport, it is not. A bus trip is made of legs, and the time of
each one depends on the clock:

1. **walk** from the origin to the stop, over the road network;
2. **wait** for the bus, which depends on when it comes;
3. **ride** the route, at the timetable's pace;
4. possibly **transfer**: walk to another stop and wait again;
5. **walk** from the last stop to the destination.

That is why a public transport router needs two things: the road network, for the
walking legs, and the **route schedules**, for the rest. `r5r` is the R interface to R5, the
Conveyal engine that does exactly this.

::: {.callout-important}
## What runs and what does not when the site is built

The blocks that call `r5r` require **JDK 21** (see @sec-r5r-java) and are not run when the
site is built. But the whole example uses the **Porto Alegre data that come inside the
package itself**: there is nothing to download, and the code runs on your machine as soon as Java
is installed. Exploring the GTFS, which does not need Java, is run as usual.
:::

```{r}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Before you start: which Java does R see? {#sec-r5r-java}

`r5r` needs **JDK 21**. There are three different questions, and the answers may not match:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# 1. which java does the system find on the PATH? (the version is on the first line)
system2("java", "-version")

# 2. which folder does the JAVA_HOME variable point to? ("" = not set)
Sys.getenv("JAVA_HOME")

# 3. which Java does rJava actually load? This is the one that counts for r5r
rJava::.jinit()
rJava::.jcall("java/lang/System", "S", "getProperty", "java.version")
```

There may be more than one Java installed on the computer. What matters is the third answer, which
should start with `21`. An error such as `JAVA_HOME cannot be determined from the Registry` means
that `rJava` did not find any Java installed.

If the version is not 21, the `rJavaEnv` package installs the JDK without needing administrator
permission and sets up the project to use it:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("rJavaEnv")
rJavaEnv::java_quick_install(version = 21)
```

Restart R after the installation and run the third check again.

## The R5 engine: the `.jar` file {#sec-r5r-jar}

`r5r` does not bundle R5. The first time it builds a network, it downloads the engine, a
`.jar` file of about 60 MB, from Conveyal's *releases* page on GitHub
(<https://github.com/conveyal/r5/releases>), and stores it in a cache folder. On later
runs, it uses the stored copy.

On the Ministry's network, this *download* may hang or fail: GitHub redirects the file
to another address (`objects.githubusercontent.com`), which the network often blocks. If
`build_network()` stops at the R5 download, first try Windows' download method,
which goes through the system proxy, like the browser:

```{r}
#| eval: false
options(download.file.method = "wininet")
r5r::download_r5()
```

If that does not work, download the `.jar` in the browser and put it in the cache folder. The link and the
folder depend on the installed version of `r5r`; this snippet shows both for your machine:

```{r}
#| eval: false
packageVersion("r5r")
r5r:::fileurl_from_metadata()                    # link to the .jar
r5r:::r5r_env$cache_dir                          # folder to paste it in
dir.create(r5r:::r5r_env$cache_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
shell.exec(r5r:::r5r_env$cache_dir)              # opens the folder in Windows Explorer
```

With `r5r` 2.4.0, which asks for R5 7.5.1, they are:

- **Link:** <https://github.com/conveyal/r5/releases/download/v7.5.1/r5-v7.5-1-gf3631e9-all.jar>
- **Folder:** `C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\R\cache\R\r5r\r5_jar_v7.5.1`

Copy the file with its original name, without renaming it.

::: {.callout-note}
## Updated `r5r`? Check the `.jar` again

Each version of `r5r` asks for a version of R5. The development version (2.4.0.9001), for
example, already asks for R5 7.6.0, in another folder (`r5_jar_v7.6.0`) and with another link. After
updating the package, run the snippet above again and, if needed, repeat the manual download.
:::

## The input: a folder with `.pbf` and GTFS

`r5r` works with a **data folder**: just put in it the OSM `.pbf` (the same as in
@sec-m4-osm) and one or more GTFS files, and it builds the network. The package's example folder:

```{r}
pasta_poa <- system.file("extdata/poa", package = "r5r")

list.files(pasta_poa, pattern = "\\.(pbf|zip)$")
```

They are the road network of a part of Porto Alegre (`poa_osm.pbf`) and two GTFS feeds: EPTC's buses
and Trensurb's metropolitan train.

## Inside the GTFS

GTFS (*General Transit Feed Specification*) is the standard format for publishing public transport
schedules. It is a `.zip` with several text tables, linked by keys.
`gtfstools` reads them all at once:

```{r}
gtfs <- gtfstools::read_gtfs(file.path(pasta_poa, "poa_eptc.zip"))

names(gtfs)
```

The tables that matter for routing:

| Table | What it has | Key that links it to the others |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `routes` | the routes (number, name, vehicle type) | `route_id` |
| `trips` | each trip of each route, in one direction | `trip_id`, `route_id`, `service_id` |
| `stops` | the stops, with coordinates | `stop_id` |
| `stop_times` | the time of each trip at each stop | `trip_id`, `stop_id` |
| `calendar` | which days each service runs, and the validity period | `service_id` |
| `shapes` | the routes' alignments, for drawing | `shape_id` |

How the tables link through the keys (`route_id`, `trip_id`, `stop_id`, `service_id`,
`shape_id`):

![Diagram of the GTFS tables and the keys that link them. Source: Ipea, repository [`gtfs2gps-time_geography`](https://github.com/ipeaGIT/gtfs2gps-time_geography).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ipeaGIT/gtfs2gps-time_geography/main/figures/flowchart_GTFS_scheme.png){#fig-gtfs-esquema fig-alt="Diagram of the GTFS schema: the agency, routes, trips, stop_times, stops, calendar and shapes tables, linked by their identifier columns."}

The routes:

```{r}
gtfs$routes |>
  dplyr::select(route_id, route_short_name, route_long_name, route_type) |>
  head()

nrow(gtfs$routes)
```

`route_type` 3 is bus. The heart of GTFS is `stop_times`, the timetable
itself:

```{r}
gtfs$stop_times |>
  dplyr::select(trip_id, stop_sequence, stop_id, arrival_time, departure_time) |>
  head(8)

nrow(gtfs$stop_times)
```

Notice the blank times: GTFS only requires the time at timing points. Between them,
R5 interpolates. And notice the size: more than 130 thousand rows just for the trips in this
extract.

`calendar` holds the information that causes the most errors:

```{r}
gtfs$calendar |> head(3)
```

This GTFS is valid from **15/04/2019 to 15/07/2019**, Monday to Friday. A query for a
Saturday, or for 2026, finds no bus at all: R5 returns walking only, without warning. The
`departure_datetime` of every query must fall within the validity period and on a service day.

A look at the stops and alignments:

```{r}
paradas   <- gtfstools::convert_stops_to_sf(gtfs)
tracados  <- gtfstools::convert_shapes_to_sf(gtfs)

c(paradas = nrow(paradas), tracados = nrow(tracados))

# mapgl wants coordinates in degrees (EPSG:4326)
paradas  <- sf::st_transform(paradas, 4326)
tracados <- sf::st_transform(tracados, 4326)

mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = tracados, height = "525px") |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(id = "Alignments", source = tracados, line_color = "#1a5b8a",
                        line_width = 1.5, tooltip = "shape_id") |>
  mapgl::add_circle_layer(id = "Stops", source = paradas, circle_color = "#b3402a",
                          circle_radius = 3, tooltip = "stop_name") |>
  mapgl::add_layers_control(position = "top-right", collapsible = FALSE)
```

### Why the departure time matters

Counting how many trips start in each hour of the day:

```{r}
#| label: fig-viagens-hora
#| fig-cap: "Bus trips started per hour of the day, EPTC GTFS (r5r sample)"
#| fig-height: 3.4
inicio_viagens <- gtfs$stop_times |>
  dplyr::filter(stop_sequence == 1) |>
  dplyr::mutate(hora = as.integer(substr(departure_time, 1, 2)))

ggplot(inicio_viagens, aes(factor(hora))) +     # each hour as a category
  geom_bar(fill = "#1a5b8a") +
  labs(x = "Trip start hour", y = "Trips") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

The figure holds a surprise: there are buses only between 11:00 and 17:50. That is not Porto
Alegre's real operation, but a cut the package makes to fit the size of an example. But it is a
useful lesson, because `r5r` does not warn you when you query a time with no service: a matrix
computed for 8:00 with this GTFS would come out with walking times only, with no error. That is why
the examples below use 14:00.

In a complete GTFS, the figure would show the typical pattern, with morning and late-afternoon peaks and
little service at night. The same trip, between the same two points, has different waiting times
depending on the hour. That is why every `r5r` result must say **for which day
and time** it was computed, and why it is worth looking at this figure before choosing the time.

## Building the network

```{r}
#| eval: false
options(java.parameters = "-Xmx2G")    # memory for Java, BEFORE loading the package
library(r5r)

# copy the example folder: R5 writes the built network (network.dat) inside it
pasta <- "dados/brutos/poa"
dir.create(pasta, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
file.copy(list.files(pasta_poa, full.names = TRUE), pasta, recursive = TRUE)

rede <- r5r::build_network(data_path = pasta)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## `setup_r5()` or `build_network()`?

Up to version 2.3, the function was called `setup_r5()`. Current versions use
`build_network()`, with the same behaviour. If your R says the function does not exist, change
the name and check with `packageVersion("r5r")`.
:::

The first time, R5 builds the network and writes `network.dat` in the folder, which can take a few
minutes for a large city. On later runs, it reuses it. Before computing anything,
check that the GTFS went in:

```{r}
#| eval: false
r5r::street_network_to_sf(rede)$edges |> nrow()      # road segments
r5r::transit_network_to_sf(rede)$routes |> nrow()    # public transport routes
```

If the second line gives zero, the GTFS was not recognised: it was unzipped, outside the folder
or malformed.

## Travel time matrix

The origin and destination points need three columns: `id`, `lon` and `lat`. The package's
example has some well-known places in Porto Alegre:

```{r}
pontos <- read.csv(file.path(pasta_poa, "poa_points_of_interest.csv"))
head(pontos)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
ttm <- r5r::travel_time_matrix(
  rede,
  origins            = pontos,
  destinations       = pontos,
  mode               = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 14:00:00",     # a Monday, within the
                                  tz = "America/Sao_Paulo"),  # GTFS validity period
  time_window        = 30,           # simulates 30 departures, minute by minute, from 14:00
  percentiles        = c(25, 50, 75),
  max_walk_time      = 20,           # maximum minutes of walking at each end
  max_trip_duration  = 90
)

head(ttm)
```

The result comes in **long format**: one row per origin–destination pair, with one
time column per percentile (`travel_time_p25`, `travel_time_p50`, `travel_time_p75`).

The arguments that change the result, and that must be stated in the report:

- **`mode`**: the main mode and the access mode. `c("WALK", "TRANSIT")` is bus with access on foot;
  `c("BICYCLE", "TRANSIT")`, with access by bike; `"CAR"` and `"WALK"` on their own also
  work.
- **`departure_datetime`**: day and time. Within the GTFS validity period, and on a day the service
  runs.
- **`time_window` and `percentiles`**: instead of a single departure time, R5 simulates every
  departure in the window and returns the distribution of times. That captures the luck of arriving at the
  stop just before or just after the bus. The 50th percentile is the usual choice; the 75th is more
  honest for people who depend on a low-frequency route.
- **`max_walk_time`** and **`walk_speed`** (default 3.6 km/h): limit and define the access
  walk. A limit that is too low leaves points without service.
- **`max_rides`**: the maximum number of boardings, that is, transfers plus one.
- **`max_trip_duration`**: cuts the matrix and speeds up the calculation a lot.

To see the effect of the time of day, just repeat the query at 18:30, when this GTFS's buses
have stopped and only the train is left, and compare:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ttm_noite <- r5r::travel_time_matrix(
  rede, origins = pontos, destinations = pontos,
  mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 18:30:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo"),
  time_window = 30, percentiles = 50, max_walk_time = 20, max_trip_duration = 90
)

dplyr::inner_join(ttm, ttm_noite, by = c("from_id", "to_id"),
                  suffix = c("_14h", "_18h30")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(diferenca_min = travel_time_p50_18h30 - travel_time_p50_14h) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(diferenca_min)) |>
  head()
```

## Detailed itineraries

The matrix says how long it takes; `detailed_itineraries()` says **how**: each leg of the trip,
with mode, route, duration and geometry.

```{r}
#| eval: false
det <- r5r::detailed_itineraries(
  rede,
  origins            = pontos[pontos$id == "farrapos_station", ],
  destinations       = pontos[pontos$id == "pucrs", ],
  mode               = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 14:00:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo"),
  shortest_path      = FALSE        # returns the alternatives, not only the fastest
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# the site does not run r5r: it loads the result of the block above, computed with the same
# example network by R/preparar_exemplos_r5r.R
det <- readRDS("dados/processados/poa/itinerario.rds")
```

Each row is a leg of one trip option:

```{r}
det |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::select(option, segment, mode, route, segment_duration, wait, distance)
```

On the map, the first option, with one colour per mode. Hover over a leg to see the
route:

```{r}
opcao <- dplyr::filter(det, option == 1)
modos <- unique(opcao$mode)
cores_modo <- c(WALK = "#7A7A7A", BUS = "#1a5b8a", RAIL = "#b3402a", SUBWAY = "#7A1F0F",
                TRAM = "#E7A07A")[modos]

mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = opcao, height = "525px") |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(
    id = "itinerario", source = opcao,
    line_color = mapgl::match_expr("mode", values = modos, stops = unname(cores_modo)),
    line_width = 5, tooltip = "route"
  ) |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Mode", values = modos, colors = unname(cores_modo), type = "categorical")
```

It is by looking at the legs (walking, waiting, riding, transferring) that you explain a travel time
that looks too high. The culprit is almost always the wait or a long walk to the stop.

## Isochrones

How far you get from a point in 15, 30 and 45 minutes:

```{r}
#| eval: false
iso <- r5r::isochrone(
  rede,
  origins            = pontos[pontos$id == "bus_central_station", ],
  mode               = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 14:00:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo"),
  cutoffs            = c(15, 30, 45)
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
iso <- readRDS("dados/processados/poa/isocronas.rds")
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
iso <- dplyr::arrange(iso, dplyr::desc(isochrone))   # the smaller bands on top

ggplot(iso) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = factor(isochrone)), alpha = 0.5, colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "YlOrRd", direction = -1, name = "minutes") +
  theme_void()
```

## Cars in `r5r`?

`r5r` also routes cars (`mode = "CAR"`), on the same network. But, like `dodgr`, it uses
free-flow speeds, and it requires Java and building the network. For cars and
freight, module 4's `dodgr` (@sec-m4-roteamento) is usually simpler and
faster.

| For... | Use |
|:--|:--|
| Road distances and times, freight, large matrices between municipalities | `dodgr` |
| Public transport, urban accessibility, isochrones, GTFS scenarios | `r5r` |
| One specific route to illustrate a map | either |

In the next chapter (@sec-m4-r5r), `r5r` comes back for a complete study: Fortaleza, with GTFS editing
to simulate an intervention and an accessibility calculation.

## From the matrix to accessibility

The time matrix says how long it takes from each place to every other. On its own, it does not yet say
whether that is good or bad: you also need to know **what exists at each destination**. The Porto Alegre example
has exactly that other half, a hexagonal grid with population and opportunities in each
hexagon:

```{r}
hex <- read.csv(file.path(pasta_poa, "poa_hexgrid.csv"))

head(hex)

c(hexagonos = nrow(hex),
  pares_od  = nrow(hex)^2)
```

Putting the two together (how long it takes from each hexagon to every other, and how many jobs,
schools or health services there are in each) is computing **accessibility**: how many
opportunities a person can reach from where they live. That is the subject of
@sec-m4-acessibilidade, after the scenario study in Fortaleza.
